sources.title: British Council — Questions and negatives
sources.conclusion: Yes/no inversion moves the first auxiliary. Negation follows it. A subject question word replaces the subject; no extra personal pronoun is needed.

sources.title: British Council — Talking about the future
sources.conclusion: Present forms can refer to scheduled or arranged futures. Will can express beliefs; prediction is not independent proof of future truth.

sources.title: Cambridge Grammar Today — Will
sources.conclusion: Statement modal order, will/subject question inversion, will not/won't; positive terminal 'll is not a standalone short-answer form.

sources.title: Cambridge Grammar Today — Contractions
sources.conclusion: Affirmative contractions do not end a clause in the relevant short-answer model. Negative terminal contractions can be used. Aliases must respect position.

sources.title: British Council — Short forms
sources.conclusion: A short answer normally repeats the first auxiliary with the dialogue's correct pronoun. Other conversational replies exist, so the target format must be specified.

sources.title: British Council — Using there is and there are
sources.conclusion: Existential there announces existence/presence. The body demonstrates is with singular and uncountable, are with plural, frequent any in negative/question patterns and there is rather than terminal there's in affirmative short answers.

sources.title: British Council — Nouns: countable and uncountable
sources.conclusion: Milk is uncountable in this use. Some and any follow typical countability/discourse patterns; some can occur in questions. Any is not universal.

sources.title: British Council Teens — There is / There are and It
sources.conclusion: Editorial dialogue distinguishes introducing existence from it/they referring to known topics and includes full existential clauses with no separate location phrase. This is editorial body, not a learner comment.

sources.title: Cambridge Grammar Today — There is, there's and there are
sources.conclusion: There is/are introduces presence. Plural there's occurs in speech and informal writing but can be incorrect in formal/examination writing. State a written-register criterion rather than a universal speech ban.

sources.title: Cambridge Grammar Today — Contractions
sources.conclusion: Affirmative contractions do not end a clause in the relevant short-answer model. Negative terminal contractions can be used. Aliases must respect position.

primary_editorial_sources.title: Present simple: 'to be'
primary_editorial_sources.editorial_scope: Grammar explanation through question-word examples, lines20–74; learner comments from line94 not used.
primary_editorial_sources.verified_claim: Present states and am/is/are agreement; pronoun contractions; not after be; I'm not and both negative contraction placements.
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Retain base forms and put alternative negative spellings in visible basic. No publisher exercise copied.

primary_editorial_sources.title: Questions and negatives
primary_editorial_sources.editorial_scope: Negative statements and be form tables, lines33–87; later learner comments not used as rules.
primary_editorial_sources.verified_claim: Not follows first verb element; ordinary present/past be statements form negatives without do-support; I am not / I'm not and is/are alternatives are listed.
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Scope the no-do statement to the taught declarative construction rather than every be use.

primary_editorial_sources.title: Be — English Grammar Today
primary_editorial_sources.verified_claim: Be has main-verb and auxiliary uses; role, quality and location models; singular profession nouns use a/an; auxiliary be forms continuous/passive constructions.
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Preserve three basic uses and show just one bounded auxiliary comparison. Do not insert be before arbitrary bare verbs.

primary_editorial_sources.title: Contractions — English Grammar Today
primary_editorial_sources.verified_claim: 's may represent is or has; ordinary I am not contracts to I'm not; she isn't/she's not and they aren't/they're not are supported; contractions are register-sensitive, not generally incorrect.
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Do not teach universal 's=is or one mandatory negative contraction. No inference about actual tone is made from full spelling alone.

primary_editorial_sources.title: Verbs: types — English Grammar Today
primary_editorial_sources.verified_claim: Linking verbs including be are followed by information about the subject, not direct objects; be also has auxiliary uses.
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: A be + adjective sentence is complete without inventing an object. Keep a short learner-friendly boundary, not a whole syntax lecture.

primary_editorial_sources.title: Nouns: form — English Grammar Today
primary_editorial_sources.verified_claim: Ordinary singular/plural noun subjects select singular/plural verbs in the displayed models.
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: Use transparent one-teacher/several-teachers/two-names examples. Do not add collective-noun or special-singular traps to A1 tasks.

primary_editorial_sources.title: Forming negative statements, questions and imperatives
primary_editorial_sources.verified_claim: Negative be statements place not/n’t after be, whereas negative imperatives use do not/don't plus base verb.
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: B no-do rule is bounded to ordinary present statements and does not invalidate accepted Don't be imperatives.

primary_editorial_sources.title: Imperative clauses (Be quiet!)
primary_editorial_sources.verified_claim: Negative imperative examples include Don't be late; imperative do-support is a different model from present declarative be.
primary_editorial_sources.conclusion: One visible boundary prevents a false global prohibition; no duplicate Imperatives lesson or course change.

metadata.prospective_learning_resource_descriptio: There is / there are повідомляє, що хтось або щось є чи наявне. Обираємо форму за іменником: однина й незлічуване — is, множина — are. Місце часто назване, але there у цій конструкції не означає обов'язково «там».
